topics.title: The Basics of the Language
topics.summary: The words you need before anything else: how to store a value, the four kinds of value, how to make a choice, how to repeat something, and how to write a function.

lesson.heading: Storing a value: let and var
lesson.body:
A program works on values: a number, a piece of text, a yes-or-no. To use a value later you have to **put it somewhere and give that place a name**. Swift gives you two ways to do that.

`let` creates a **constant**: you give it a value once, and from then on it can never change.

`var` creates a **variable**: you can give it a different value later, as many times as you want.

Which one should you use? **Start with `let` every time**, and only switch to `var` when you actually need to change the value. A value that cannot change is a value that cannot surprise you later, and that is half of what makes code easy to read.

You also never have to say what kind of value it is. Swift looks at what you wrote on the right of the `=` and works it out by itself. This is called **type inference** — "inferring" just means "figuring out from the clues".

If you try to change something made with `let`, the **compiler** (the program that turns your code into an app) refuses to build it, and tells you why.
lesson.code:
let pi = 3.14        // a number with decimals, and it stays 3.14 forever
var counter = 0      // a whole number that we will change
counter += 1         // same as: counter = counter + 1

let name: String     // here we only say "a piece of text is coming"
name = "Ada"         // and we give it its one and only value here

// pi = 3.15         // this line would not build: pi was made with let

lesson.heading: The four kinds of value you will use all the time
lesson.body:
Every value in Swift has a **type**: the kind of thing it is. Four of them cover almost everything you write at the beginning.

`Int` is a whole number: `3`, `0`, `-17`.
`Double` is a number with a decimal point: `2.5`, `3.14`.
`Bool` is a yes-or-no: only `true` or `false`.
`String` is text: `"Ada"`, `"hello"`. Text always goes between double quotes.

There is one rule here that surprises everybody at first: **Swift never turns one type into another behind your back**. If you try to add an `Int` and a `Double`, it refuses. You have to say it out loud: `Double(a)` makes a `Double` out of `a`.

It is annoying for a week. Then you realise a whole family of bugs — the ones where a number silently loses its decimals — simply does not exist in Swift.

The other thing to watch: when you divide two `Int`, the result is an `Int` too. `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. The part after the dot is thrown away, not rounded. If you want `3.5`, at least one of the two has to be a `Double`.

Finally, to put a value inside some text, write `\(...)` with the value in the middle. That is called **string interpolation**, and whatever you put inside the brackets is worked out first.
lesson.code:
let a = 3            // Int: whole number
let b = 2.5          // Double: has decimals

// let c = a + b     // does not build: an Int and a Double are not the same type
let c = Double(a) + b   // 5.5 — now they are both Double

print(7 / 2)         // 3   — two Int, so the result is an Int: the .5 is thrown away
print(7.0 / 2)       // 3.5 — one of them is a Double, so the result is a Double

let name = "Ada"
print("Hello \(name), you have \(2 + 3) messages")
// prints: Hello Ada, you have 5 messages

lesson.heading: Making a choice: if and switch
lesson.body:
`if` runs some code only when a condition is true. In Swift the condition has to be an actual `Bool` — a real true or false. In some other languages the number `1` counts as "true"; **in Swift it does not**, and `if 1` does not build. That removes a classic source of confusion.

After `if` you can add `else`, which runs when the condition is false.

`switch` is for when you are comparing one value against several possibilities. Instead of a chain of `if`, you list the cases. Three things make Swift's `switch` different from the one in older languages:

**It must cover everything.** Either you list every possible value, or you add `default`, which means "anything else". If you forget a case, the compiler stops you.

**It does not slide into the next case.** In C and Java, a case keeps running into the one below unless you write `break`. In Swift it stops on its own. If you *want* it to continue, you write `fallthrough` yourself — and that word is rare in real code.

**It can match more than single values.** `..<6` means "anything below 6". `6...7` means "6 or 7". `where` adds an extra condition to a case.

lesson.heading: Repeating something: loops
lesson.body:
A **loop** repeats a piece of code. The one you will write most is `for-in`: it goes through a series of values one at a time, and each time around it hands you the current one.

That series can be a **range** of numbers, a list of things, or the letters of a piece of text.

Ranges have two shapes, and the difference matters:

`1...5` includes 5. Three dots, both ends in.
`1..<5` stops at 4. Two dots and a `<`, the last one is left out.

Mixing these two up is the single most common small mistake in Swift — the result is off by one. Read `..<` as "up to, but not including".

If you do not need the value itself, only the number of repetitions, write `_` instead of a name. The underscore means "I know something arrives here and I do not want it".

There are also `while` and `repeat-while`, which repeat as long as a condition stays true. You see them rarely: `for-in` covers almost everything.
lesson.code:
var total = 0
for i in 1..<4 {     // i is 1, then 2, then 3 — 4 is left out
    total += i
}
print(total)         // 6, because 1 + 2 + 3

for _ in 0..<3 {     // just do this three times
    print("hi")
}

for c in "abc" {     // c is "a", then "b", then "c"
    print(c)
}

lesson.heading: Writing a function
lesson.body:
A **function** is a piece of code with a name, which you can run whenever you want. You write it once and call it as many times as you like.

You declare it with `func`. In the brackets go the **parameters**: the values the function needs in order to do its job, each with its type. After `->` goes the type of the value it hands back. If there is nothing to hand back, you leave `->` out.

Swift has one feature here that other languages do not: **every parameter has two names**. The first is the **label**, which you write when you call the function; the second is the name used inside the function's body. The point is that the call reads like a sentence: `sum(2, with: 3)`.

If you only write one name, it is used for both. If you write `_` as the label, there is no label at all at the call site.

A parameter can have a **default value**: if you do not pass it, that value is used. And if the body is a single expression, you can leave out the word `return`.

questions.prompt: What happens when you try to build this code?
questions.code:
let x = 10
x = 20
print(x)
options: It prints 10 and shows a warning
questions.explanation: `let` makes a constant: it gets its value once and never again. The second line tries to give it a new one, and the compiler refuses to build the app. Nothing runs, so nothing is printed. To be able to change it you would have to write `var x = 10`.
whyWrong: That would be true with `var x = 10`. With `let`, the line `x = 20` never becomes part of the app: the build stops first, so `print` is never reached.
Nothing gets printed at all. The problem is not that Swift ignores the second line — it is that the app is never built in the first place.
A warning is a suggestion: the app still gets built and still runs. This is an error, which is stronger: there is no app at the end of it.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let n = 7
let m = 2
print(n / m)
questions.explanation: Both `n` and `m` are whole numbers (`Int`), so Swift does a whole-number division: it keeps the 3 and throws away what is left over. To get 3.5 at least one of the two has to be a `Double`, for example `Double(n) / Double(m)`.
whyWrong: 3.5 is what you get when you divide numbers with decimals. Here both are `Int`, and `Int` divided by `Int` gives an `Int`. You have to ask for decimals: `Double(n) / Double(m)`.
The leftover is **thrown away**, not rounded up. 3.5 becomes 3, never 4. If you want rounding you have to ask for it: `(Double(n) / Double(m)).rounded()`.
The code is perfectly valid — dividing two `Int` is allowed. The trap is in the result, not in whether it builds.

questions.prompt: What happens when you try to build this code?
questions.code:
let a = 3
let b = 2.5
print(a + b)
questions.explanation: Swift decided on its own that `a` is an `Int` and `b` is a `Double`, and it never converts one into the other by itself. There is simply no `+` that takes an `Int` on one side and a `Double` on the other. You have to write the conversion yourself: `Double(a) + b`.
whyWrong: 5.5 is what you would get if Swift quietly turned `a` into a `Double`, the way C or Java do. Swift deliberately does not: you write `Double(a) + b` and it is clear to anyone reading.
Nothing is cut off, because the addition never happens. The compiler stops before that, when it cannot find a `+` between an `Int` and a `Double`.
The problem is not what shape the result has. The problem is that `a + b` does not exist as long as the two sides are different types.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let name = "Ada"
print("Hello \(name), you have \(2 + 3) messages")
questions.explanation: Writing `\(...)` inside text means "work out what is in here and put the result in". So `name` becomes `Ada`, and `2 + 3` is calculated first and becomes `5`. This is called string interpolation.
whyWrong: That is the text exactly as typed. To print it literally you would need a raw string, written `#"..."#`. With normal quotes, `\(` always starts an interpolation.
What goes inside `\(...)` is not text, it is something to calculate. `2 + 3` is worked out and becomes `5` before it ever reaches the final string.
The code is fine. Interpolation accepts anything you can calculate, arithmetic included.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `1..<4` means "from 1 up to, but not including, 4". So `i` is 1, then 2, then 3. Adding them up: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
whyWrong: 10 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, which is what `1...4` with three dots would give you. The `<` in `..<` is exactly what keeps 4 out.
3 is how many times the loop runs, not what it adds up to. Each time around it adds `i` — 1, then 2, then 3 — not 1 each time.
4 is the number that gets left out. Mixing up `..<` with `...` is the most common small slip in Swift: read `..<` as "up to, but not including".

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let n = 1
switch n {
case 1:
    print("one")
    fallthrough
case 2:
    print("two")
default:
    print("other")
}
questions.explanation: In Swift a `switch` stops at the end of the case that matched: normally this would print only `one`. The word `fallthrough` says "carry on into the next case anyway", so `two` is printed too. Then it stops, because that second case has no `fallthrough` of its own.
whyWrong: `only one` is what you would get without that `fallthrough` line. It is there on purpose, and it forces the jump into the case below.
`fallthrough` carries you into the **next** case, one single step. The case printing `two` has no `fallthrough`, so `default` is never reached.
`fallthrough` is a real Swift keyword and it is used correctly here. It is just rare, because Swift was designed so you almost never need it.

questions.prompt: Given this function, which call is the correct one?
questions.explanation: Each parameter has two names: the one you write when calling, and the one used inside. The first parameter has `_` as its calling name, which means "no label here". The second has `with` for calling and `b` inside. So the call is `sum(2, with: 3)`.
whyWrong: `a` is the name used **inside** the function, not when calling it. The `_` in front of it removes the label from the call, so `a:` must not appear.
The second parameter's label is not optional: `with:` was written on purpose and has to be there. Only the first one is label-free, thanks to the `_`.
Neither label is right: the first one must not be written at all, and the second is `with`, not `b`. `b` only exists inside the function's body.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let grade = 7
switch grade {
case ..<6:
    print("failing")
case 6...7:
    print("passing")
case let v where v >= 9:
    print("excellent")
default:
    print("good")
}
questions.explanation: The cases are checked from the top down, and the **first** one that matches wins. 7 is not under 6, but it is inside `6...7`, so `passing` is printed and the switch ends right there.
whyWrong: `default` only runs when nothing above it matched. Here `6...7` matched first, so the switch never gets that far — `good` would be for an 8.
`..<6` means "below 6", and 7 is not below 6. So that case does not match.
A `switch` runs one single case and then stops. Two of them run only if you write `fallthrough` yourself, and there is none here.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let x = Int8.max
print(x &+ 1)
questions.explanation: `Int8` is a very small whole number: it only has room for values from -128 to 127. `Int8.max` is 127. The `&+` operator means "add, and if it does not fit, start again from the other end" — so from 127 you land on -128. The normal `+` would have crashed the app instead, on purpose, so the mistake does not go unnoticed.
whyWrong: 128 simply does not fit in an `Int8`: the largest value it can hold is 127. That is the whole reason the number wraps around.
127 is the starting point, before adding 1. `&+` does add — it just lands somewhere unexpected because the box is too small.
A crash is what the normal `+` would do. The `&` in front is exactly the way to say "I know it can overflow, wrap it around instead of stopping".

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let s = "e\u{301}"   // the letter 'e' followed by an accent mark
print(s.count)
questions.explanation: In Swift, counting a `String` counts **what a reader sees**, not how it is stored. Here the letter `e` and the accent mark join into a single visible character, `é`, so the answer is 1. In most other languages the same text would count as 2, because they count storage units rather than visible characters.
whyWrong: 2 is what you get if you count the pieces it is stored as. Swift deliberately counts differently: one visible character counts as one.
3 would be the number of bytes needed to store it in memory. That is `s.utf8.count`, a different question entirely.
The text is not empty: there is a visible `é` in it. 0 would mean nothing is there at all.

topics.title: Optionals: the value that might not be there
topics.summary: How Swift says "here there might be nothing", and why that one idea removes the most common crash in every other language.

lesson.heading: The problem optionals solve
lesson.body:
Think of a form where the phone number is not required. When you read that field, two things can happen: there is a number, or there is nothing at all.

Almost every programming language handles "nothing" with a special value — `null`, `nil`, `None` — and almost every language lets you use it by mistake as if it were a real value. The app then stops dead. It happens so often that the man who invented the idea publicly called it his "billion dollar mistake".

Swift fixes it in a simple way: **a normal type can never be nothing**. If you write `String`, there is text in there, guaranteed. Always.

When something might be missing, you add a question mark: `String?`. That is an **optional**, and it means "either a piece of text, or nothing". The two are different types, and Swift will not let you mix them up.

The effect is that the mistake moves from the running app to your screen while you are writing. The compiler stops you and says "this might be empty, decide what to do". You cannot forget, because it does not let you.

lesson.heading: What an optional is underneath
lesson.body:
The question mark is not magic, and it is not a special kind of pointer. It is a plain type that Swift's standard library writes in ordinary Swift, and you could have written it yourself.

It is an **enum**: a type that lists the few shapes a value is allowed to have. `Optional` has exactly two:

`.none` — there is nothing here.
`.some(value)` — there is something, and here it is, kept inside.

So `Int?` is really "either nothing, or a box with an `Int` in it". The word `nil` is just a friendlier way of writing `.none`, and `5` written into an `Int?` is really `.some(5)`.

This is worth knowing for two reasons. First, in an interview it is asked constantly. Second, it explains **unwrapping**: taking the value out of the box. The box and the thing inside are not the same, which is why you cannot use one where the other is expected.

lesson.heading: Opening the box safely
lesson.body:
To use what is inside, you have to open the box, and Swift wants you to say what happens if it turns out to be empty. There are three everyday ways.

**`if let`** — "if there is something in there, give it this name and run this block". Inside the block the value is a normal, guaranteed one. Outside, the name does not exist.

**`guard let`** — the same check, but the other way round: "if there is nothing, leave now". The difference that matters is that the name **stays alive for the rest of the function**, instead of only inside a block. This is what keeps real code flat: all the leaving-early at the top, then the real work with no indentation.

**`?.` (optional chaining)** — "go on only if there is something; otherwise the whole expression is nothing". Useful for going down a chain: `user?.address?.street`. Watch out: as soon as there is one `?` anywhere in the chain, the **whole result** becomes optional, even the part at the end that could never be empty.

lesson.heading: A value to fall back on, and the dangerous shortcut
lesson.body:
Often you do not want to branch: you just want a fallback value when the real one is missing. That is `??`, the **nil-coalescing operator**: "this, or if it is empty, that".

The right-hand side is only worked out **if it is needed**. If the left side has a value, the right side never runs. That matters when the right side is an expensive function call.

Then there is `!`, **force unwrapping**: "take it out, and if it is empty, stop the app". It is a deliberate crash. Sometimes that is right — a resource you yourself put in the app, which can only be missing if you made a mistake — but every `!` in your code is a promise. If you cannot explain in one sentence why it can never be empty, use `??` or `if let` instead.

Finally there is `String!`, the **implicitly unwrapped optional**. It is still an optional, but it opens itself whenever it is used. It exists almost only for `@IBOutlet`: a view from a storyboard that is empty for a moment at the start and full for the whole rest of its life. Do not use it anywhere else.

lesson.heading: Transforming without opening: map and flatMap
lesson.body:
Sometimes you want to change what is inside the box without taking it out — and if the box is empty, nothing should happen.

**`map`** does exactly that: "if there is something, run this on it; if not, stay empty". The result is a box with the new value inside.

There is a trap. If the thing you run **itself returns an optional**, you end up with a box inside a box: `Int??`. That is almost never what you want, and it is a classic interview question.

**`flatMap`** is the same, but it flattens the two boxes into one: `Int?`. The rule of thumb: use `map` when what you return is always there, `flatMap` when what you return might itself be missing.

You can also match an optional like any other enum, with `if case .some(let x)`. Nobody writes that in real code — `if let` is shorter and means the same thing — but it shows that the "box" idea is literally true.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let a: Int? = nil
print(a ?? 5)
questions.explanation: `??` means "use the value on the left, and if it is empty use the one on the right". `a` is empty, so 5 is used. The result is a normal `Int`, not an optional one: `??` has already dealt with the empty case.
whyWrong: `nil` is what `a` holds, but `??` is there precisely so that nothing empty ever comes out. Printing `a` on its own would show `nil`.
The `Optional(...)` wrapper appears when you print a box that is still closed. `??` opens it and hands back a plain `Int`, so there is no wrapper.
The code is fine. `??` between an `Int?` on the left and an `Int` on the right is exactly what it is for.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let s: String? = "hello"
print(s)
questions.explanation: `s` is a still-closed box, and printing it shows the box too: `Optional("hello")`. Xcode even warns you about it, because printing an optional is almost always a sign that you forgot to open it. To get just `hello`, open it first with `if let` or `??`.
whyWrong: `hello` is what is inside, but nobody took it out. You would get it with `print(s ?? "")` or inside an `if let`.
The quotes do not appear in `print`: that is how the debugger shows text, not how it is printed.
It builds and runs. It only produces a warning suggesting you open the optional on purpose.

questions.prompt: How is `Optional` actually built in Swift's standard library?
options: A pointer that can be NULL
An enum with two cases, `.none` and `.some(Wrapped)`
A protocol that every type adopts
questions.explanation: It is an ordinary enum, written in normal Swift: `.none` for nothing, `.some(x)` for something. `nil` is a friendlier way of writing `.none`. That is also why the value has to be taken out of the case before you can use it.
whyWrong: A pointer that may be NULL is the C approach, and it is exactly the one Swift wanted to get away from. An enum carries no pointer, and works with structs and numbers too.
It is not a class, which matters: an optional is a value type, so it is copied rather than shared, and it costs nothing extra in memory.
There is no protocol here. Any type at all can be made optional, without the type having to agree to anything.

questions.prompt: What is the real difference between `guard let` and `if let`?
options: With `guard let` the name stays usable after the check
`guard let` is faster when the app runs
`if let` does not work with properties
questions.explanation: Both check the same thing. The difference is where the opened value lives: with `if let` only inside the braces, with `guard let` for the whole rest of the function. That is why `guard` is used to leave early at the top, leaving the real work flat and unindented below.
whyWrong: There is no difference in speed: it is exactly the same check. The difference is only in how the code is shaped and how far the name reaches.
`if let` works with anything optional, properties included. There is no such restriction.
Both work with anything: structs, enums, numbers, text. Optionals have nothing to do with classes.

questions.prompt: `street` is a normal `String`, never empty. What type is `n`?
questions.code: let n = user?.address?.street.count
questions.explanation: When you walk down a chain with `?.`, the **whole result** becomes optional, because any link in the chain might be missing. There are two `?` here, but the levels do not stack up: the answer is a single `Int?`. If `user` or `address` is missing, `n` is `nil`.
whyWrong: A plain `Int` would mean the chain can never break. But if `user` is missing there is no number to count, so something must stand for "nothing".
Two question marks do not give two levels of box: optional chaining deliberately flattens them into one. Boxes inside boxes come from `map`, not from `?.`.
`String?` is the type of `street` seen through the chain. But `.count` is called on it, and `.count` gives a number.

questions.prompt: What type is `r`?
questions.code:
let s: String? = "42"
let r = s.map { Int($0) }
questions.explanation: `map` wraps whatever you hand back in a box. What you hand back here is `Int("42")`, which is already a box, because the text might not be a number. Box inside a box: `Int??`. Use `flatMap` instead and you get a single `Int?`.
whyWrong: `Int?` is what `flatMap` gives you, because it flattens the two levels. `map` does not: it wraps what it gets, whatever shape it is.
A plain `Int` would mean two things can never fail: `s` being empty, and the text not being a number. Both can.
`String?` is what we started from. `map` has changed the content into a number.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `??` only works out its right-hand side **if it has to**. `v` has 3 in it, so the fallback is never called and never prints anything. This laziness is deliberate: it lets you put an expensive call on the right without paying for it when it is not needed.
whyWrong: That would be true if `??` worked out both sides first. It does not: it looks left, and only reaches right if there is nothing there.
0 would come out only if `v` were empty. It holds 3, so the fallback value never enters the picture.
`??` hands back a plain `Int`, already opened. The `Optional(...)` wrapper only shows up when you print an unopened box.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: This is `if let` written the long way. An optional is an enum, so you can match it like any other: `.some(let y)` means "if there is something in there, call it `y`". `y` is a normal `Int`, so it prints 5.
whyWrong: `y` is what was inside the box, already taken out — a plain `Int`. The wrapper only shows if you print the box itself.
`x` is not empty, so the case matches and the block runs. Nothing would be printed only if `x` were `nil`.
It builds: `Optional` really is an enum with those two cases, so this matching is valid. It is just a long-winded way of writing `if let y = x`.

questions.prompt: What type does Swift give `copy` here?
questions.code:
var name: String! = "Ada"
let copy = name
questions.explanation: `String!` is still an optional — it just opens itself automatically where a normal `String` is expected. Here nothing requires a `String`, so Swift keeps the safe reading and gives `copy` the type `String?`. The `!` does not travel with it.
whyWrong: It would be `String` if the line forced it, for example `let copy: String = name`. With nothing to force it, Swift stays on the safe side.
`!` is not a type that gets passed along: it is a note on that one declaration saying "open me when needed". It does not spread to new names.
It builds without complaint. The surprise is only in the type you end up with.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let dict: [String: Int?] = ["a": nil]
print(dict["a"] == nil)
questions.explanation: There are two levels of "nothing" here. Looking something up in a dictionary already gives an optional, because the key might not be there. The stored values are themselves optional. So `dict["a"]` is `Int??`: the key **was** found, and what it held was an empty box. Found means not `nil`, so the answer is `false`.
whyWrong: `true` would mean the key was not in the dictionary at all. It is there — what is stored under it happens to be empty, which is a different thing.
A comparison with `==` always gives `true` or `false`. It cannot give `nil`.
It builds. Having a box inside a box is allowed; it is just confusing, which is exactly why it gets asked about.

topics.title: Copying or sharing: struct and class
topics.summary: What really happens when you assign one thing to another: with a struct you get a copy, with a class you share the same thing. Everything else follows from that.

lesson.heading: Copy or share: the one difference that matters
lesson.body:
In Swift there are two families of types, and telling them apart is the first thing you get asked about.

**`struct` and `enum` are value types.** When you assign one to a new name, or pass it to a function, Swift makes a **copy**. From that moment they are two separate things: changing one leaves the other exactly as it was.

**`class` is a reference type.** Assigning does not copy anything: both names end up pointing at the **same** thing in memory. Change it through one name and you see the change through the other too, because there is only one thing there.

A picture that helps: a struct is a sheet of paper you photocopy, a class is a whiteboard in a room. Give someone the photocopy and they can scribble on it without touching yours. Tell them where the room is and you are both writing on the same board.

Why does Swift lean so hard on structs? Because the surprises in large codebases almost always come from sharing: something changes under your feet because another part of the program is holding the same object. With a copy that cannot happen.
lesson.code:
struct P { var x = 0 }    // value: gets copied
class  R { var x = 0 }    // reference: gets shared

var p1 = P()
var p2 = p1               // copy made here
p2.x = 1
print(p1.x)               // 0 — p1 was never touched

let r1 = R()
let r2 = r1               // no copy: same object, two names
r2.x = 1
print(r1.x)               // 1 — there was only ever one object

lesson.heading: Why let means two different things
lesson.body:
`let` always means the same thing: **this name cannot be pointed at something else**. What changes is what that implies, and it depends on which family the type belongs to.

On a **struct**, the value *is* the thing in the box. Making it constant freezes the whole thing: you cannot change its fields either. `let s = S(); s.v = 2` does not build.

On a **class**, the box holds a direction to the object, not the object itself. Making it constant freezes the direction, not what is at the other end. `let c = C(); c.v = 2` builds perfectly: you have not changed where it points, you have changed what is there.

From the same idea comes the word **`mutating`**. A method on a struct that changes one of its own fields is really replacing the whole value, so you have to say so in front: `mutating func`. It is not red tape — it is the compiler telling you "this method cannot be called on a constant", before you find out the hard way.

Classes never need `mutating`: there is nothing to replace, you are writing on the whiteboard.

lesson.heading: Copying an array is cheaper than it looks
lesson.body:
If every assignment of a struct copies it, and an array is a struct, does copying a list of a million items copy a million items?

No — and the trick has a name: **copy-on-write**, which means "copy only when somebody writes".

When you assign an array to another name, Swift copies nothing: both names quietly share the same memory. It also keeps a count of how many names are sharing it. The moment one of them tries to **change** something, Swift checks that count: if somebody else is still looking, it makes the real copy first, and only then applies the change.

So you get the behaviour of a value — nobody sees anyone else's changes — at the cost of a reference, as long as you only read.

`Array`, `String`, `Dictionary` and `Set` all do this for you. You only need to write it by hand if you build your own type holding a large buffer, and the tool for it is `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`, which answers exactly the question "am I the only one holding this?".

lesson.heading: Which one should you reach for
lesson.body:
The practical rule: **start with a struct**. Use a class only when you need something a struct cannot do.

A struct fits when the thing *is* its data: a point, a date, a model you decoded from the network, the state of a screen. Two of them with the same fields are the same thing, and nobody needs to "follow" a particular one.

A class is the right answer when:

**Identity matters.** Two users with identical names are still two different people, and you need to be able to ask "is this the same one?". That is what `===` is for: not "are they equal" but "are they literally the same object".

**It has a life of its own.** A network client, a database, a thing that holds a connection open.

**Something else requires it.** Inheriting from a UIKit class, being watched by `@Observable`, talking to an Objective-C API.

One last corner: a struct **cannot contain itself**. A node that holds another node of the same kind would need infinite room. The keyword `indirect` solves it by storing that part separately, and it is exactly why recursive enums need it.

lesson.heading: What a closure captures
lesson.body:
A **closure** is a block of code you can save and run later. When it mentions something from outside itself, it **captures** it — it takes it along.

Here the two families behave differently again, and it surprises everybody once.

If you capture a **struct**, the closure takes a copy, right then and there. Change the original afterwards and the closure will still show you the old value, because it is holding its own copy.

If you capture a **class**, the closure takes the direction to the object. Change the object afterwards and the closure sees the change, because there is only one object.

The difference is not about closures — it is the same copy-versus-share rule as everywhere else. But because the closure runs later, the two get told apart much more clearly.

lesson.heading: Two things people get wrong
lesson.body:
**"Structs live on the stack, classes on the heap."** This is the sentence you hear most, and it is not reliable. The stack is the quick scratch space of a function; the heap is longer-lived memory. A struct often does live on the stack, but not when it is inside a class, inside an array, or captured by a closure — then it lives wherever its container does. The compiler decides, and it is allowed to change its mind. Say instead what you actually know: **structs are copied, classes are shared**.

**"Structs are always faster."** Usually yes, because no extra memory has to be reserved and nothing has to be counted. But a very large struct, passed around a lot, means copying a lot of bytes. And classes have a cost structs do not: every time a reference is taken or dropped, a counter goes up or down. In practice: choose by meaning first, and measure before changing anything for speed.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `P` is a struct, so `var b = a` makes a copy. From that line onwards they are two separate things: changing `b` does not touch `a`, which still holds its starting value, 0.
whyWrong: 5 is what `b` holds. It would also be `a` if `P` were a class, because then there would be one single object with two names.
`nil` means "nothing here", and that cannot happen: `x` is a normal `Int` that starts at 0.
The code is fine. Assigning and changing a struct is the most ordinary thing there is.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `P` is a class, so `let b = a` copies nothing: `a` and `b` are two names for the same object. Changing `x` through `b` changes the only object there is, and `a` sees 5.
whyWrong: 0 is what you would get with a struct, where the assignment makes a copy. With a class there is no copy to make.
`x` is a normal `Int` starting at 0: it can never be "nothing".
It builds. `let` freezes the name, not the object it points to — see the next question.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
questions.explanation: In a struct the value *is* the thing itself, so `let` freezes all of it, fields included. Changing `v` would mean replacing the whole value, and that is not allowed on a constant. With `var s = S()` it would work.
whyWrong: 2 would need the change to go through. The compiler stops it: with a struct, touching a field means replacing the value.
It does not even get as far as printing. The build fails before the app exists.
A crash happens while the app is running. Here the app is never built, so there is nothing to run.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: With a class, `let` freezes the direction, not what is at the end of it. You have not pointed `c` at a different object — you have changed a field of the object it already points to. That is allowed, and the answer is 2.
whyWrong: 1 would be the answer if the change had not gone through. It did: `v` is declared `var` inside the class.
It builds. What `let` would forbid is `c = C()`, pointing the name at a new object.
Nothing crashes: writing to a `var` field of a live object is completely ordinary.

questions.prompt: When is the array's memory actually copied?
questions.code:
var a = [1, 2, 3]
var b = a
b.append(4)
options: On the first change to `b`, so on `append`
Never: `a` and `b` share the memory forever
When `a` is no longer in use
questions.explanation: This is copy-on-write. The assignment copies nothing: both names share the same memory and Swift simply notes that two names are looking at it. The copy only happens when `append` is about to change things and Swift sees that somebody else is still watching.
whyWrong: Copying straight away is what a naive value type would do, and it would make every array assignment expensive. Swift waits until it has to.
They cannot share forever, otherwise `append` on `b` would show up in `a` — and an array is a value type, so that must never happen.
It has nothing to do with `a` ending its life. What triggers the copy is a change, and only while more than one name is holding the memory.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The copy of a struct is **shallow**: it copies the fields as they are. The field here is a direction to a `Box`, so both copies end up pointing at the **same** box. Changing `v` goes through to both. This is the classic trap of a struct holding a class.
whyWrong: 0 is what you would expect if the copy went all the way down. It does not: Swift copies the field, which is a direction, not the object at the other end.
`v` is a normal `Int` starting at 0, so it can never be "nothing".
It builds fine. The trap is in the result, not in whether it compiles.

questions.prompt: What does the `===` operator check?
options: Whether two structs have the same fields
Whether two types are the same
Whether two names point to the same object
questions.explanation: `===` asks about identity, not equality: "are these two names pointing at literally the same object?". It only works with classes, because only there does the question make sense. For "do they hold the same thing" you use `==`.
whyWrong: That is `==`, which compares contents. Two different objects can perfectly well be equal.
Comparing fields is also `==`, and structs cannot be used with `===` at all: there is no object to identify.
Comparing types is a different question, and the tool for it is `type(of:)` or `is`.

questions.prompt: Why does a recursive enum need `indirect`?
options: Without it, its size would never settle on a number
To turn it into a reference type
questions.explanation: The compiler needs to know how much room a value takes. If a case of the enum contains the enum itself, the sum never ends: each one contains another one. `indirect` breaks the loop by storing that case's contents separately, so the value itself only has to hold a direction, which has a known size.
whyWrong: Pattern matching works with every enum, recursive or not. `indirect` has nothing to do with it.
The enum stays a value type: it is still copied. Only the storage of that one case moves elsewhere.
`Equatable` comes from writing it in the list of what the type conforms to, and has nothing to do with recursion.

questions.prompt: Which function do you use to write copy-on-write by hand in your own struct?
questions.explanation: It answers exactly the question you need: "am I the only one holding this?". If the answer is yes you can change the memory in place; if not, you copy first and then change. That is the whole of copy-on-write.
whyWrong: That is for working with raw memory directly. It says nothing about how many people are holding a reference.
`ObjectIdentifier` gives an object a unique label, useful for comparing or putting in a set. It does not count who is holding it.
That is an old Objective-C runtime function. Its result is not trustworthy in Swift, and it must not be used for this.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: A closure capturing a `var` captures **the variable itself**, not a snapshot of its value. So when `f` finally runs, it reads `p` as it is at that moment, which is 7. To freeze the value as it was you would write a capture list: `{ [p] in print(p.x) }`.
whyWrong: 0 is what you get with a capture list, `[p]`, which copies the value at the moment the closure is created. Without it, the variable is shared.
It builds: capturing a variable in a closure is completely normal.
It does not depend on anything: the rule is fixed and the result is always the same. Swift has no "it depends" in its semantics here.

topics.title: Closures: code you can hand around
topics.summary: A block of code saved in a name: how to write one, what it takes with it, and why the word `self` inside one deserves attention.

lesson.heading: What a closure is, and the short way to write it
lesson.body:
A **closure** is a piece of code you can put in a name, pass to a function and run later. Think of a function without a name, which you can hand to somebody else: "here, run this when you are done".

You see them everywhere: sorting a list ("use this rule to compare"), transforming one ("do this to every item"), reacting to a button, being told that a download has finished.

Swift lets you shorten them a lot, and the short forms confuse beginners because they look like magic. They are not — here is the full version and then each thing that gets dropped:

`{ (n: Int) -> Int in return n * 2 }` is the whole thing: parameters, what it gives back, then `in`, then the body.

The types can go, because Swift already knows them from where you are passing it. The `return` can go if the body is a single expression. The names can go, replaced by `$0`, `$1` and so on, in order. And if the closure is the last thing you pass to a function, it can jump outside the brackets. That last one is called a **trailing closure**, and it is what makes `map { $0 * 2 }` read the way it does.

lesson.heading: What it takes with it: capturing
lesson.body:
The name "closure" comes from this: when the block mentions something from outside itself, it **closes over** it — it keeps hold of it, so that it still works later, even when whatever created it is long gone.

And here is the thing that trips everyone up at least once. By default, a closure captures **the variable itself, not the value it had**. So if the variable changes afterwards, the closure sees the new value, not the one from when it was written.

If you want to freeze the value as it is right now, you write a **capture list**: the square brackets at the start, `{ [n] in ... }`. That makes a copy on the spot, and from then on the closure has its own private one.

One detail worth keeping straight: a capture list copies **the value in the box**. For a struct that means a real copy. For a class it means a copy of the direction to the object — so you still reach the same object, and changes to it are still visible. Capture lists freeze which object you are looking at, not what is inside it.

lesson.heading: Closures that outlive the call: @escaping
lesson.body:
When you pass a closure to a function, there are two things that function might do with it.

It might run it **right away** and be done, as `map` does. The closure never outlives the call. That is **non-escaping**, and it is the default.

Or it might **keep it for later**: save it in a property, add it to a list, hand it to a download that finishes in two seconds. The closure escapes the function and survives it. For that you have to write `@escaping` in front of its type.

Why does Swift insist on the distinction? Because of what it means for memory and for safety. A non-escaping closure is guaranteed to be finished by the time the function returns, so Swift can put it on the quick scratch memory, let it change local variables directly, and — most importantly — **guarantee it cannot create a memory leak**.

That guarantee is the reason you do not need `[weak self]` with `map` or `sorted`, and the reason you often do with a completion handler. If the closure cannot survive the call, it cannot keep anything alive.

lesson.heading: When a closure keeps an object alive forever
lesson.body:
Swift frees an object when nobody is holding it any more. It counts the holders: when the count hits zero, the memory goes back.

A closure that escapes **is** a holder. So this can happen: an object holds a closure, and that closure mentions the object. Each is keeping the other alive, the count never reaches zero, and neither is ever freed. That is a **retain cycle**, and it is a leak.

The fix is to tell the closure not to count as a holder:

**`[weak self]`** — "hold it, but do not count". Inside, `self` becomes optional, because by the time the closure runs the object may be gone. You almost always start with `guard let self else { return }`.

**`[unowned self]`** — the same, but without the optional, on your promise that the object will still be there. If you are wrong, the app crashes. Use it only when the lifetimes are plainly tied together.

The practical advice: `weak` by default, `unowned` only when you can explain why it is safe. And remember you only need either of them when the closure escapes **and** the object is holding it back.

lesson.heading: Code that only runs if it is needed: @autoclosure
lesson.body:
Sometimes you want a value only **if** it is actually going to be used, and working it out costs something.

The classic case is logging. `log(expensiveDescription(), enabled: false)` works out the description first and then throws it away: the cost is paid for nothing.

Writing `@autoclosure` in front of a parameter means: "whoever calls this writes a normal value, and Swift quietly wraps it in a closure". The function then decides whether to run it. So the call stays readable, and the work only happens if it is needed.

You have used this without knowing it. `??` is built this way: `a ?? expensive()` does not touch the right-hand side when the left has a value. The same goes for `assert` and `precondition`, which do nothing at all in a release build.

Use it sparingly in your own code. It makes the call site lie a little — something that looks like a plain value might not run — and that is only worth it when skipping the work genuinely matters.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
var n = 1
let f = { print(n) }
n = 2
f()
questions.explanation: By default a closure captures **the variable**, not a snapshot of its value. When `f` finally runs, it goes and reads `n` as it is at that moment, which is 2. To freeze the 1 you would write `{ [n] in print(n) }`.
whyWrong: 1 is what you get with a capture list, `[n]`, which copies the value when the closure is created. Without it, the variable is shared.
`n` is a normal `Int` that always holds a number. There is no "nothing" here.
It builds: a closure reading a variable from around it is the most ordinary thing there is.

questions.prompt: When do you have to write `@escaping`?
options: When the closure returns a value
When the closure might run after the function has returned
Always, for any closure that takes parameters
questions.explanation: `@escaping` means "this closure can outlive the call": it gets saved in a property, put in a list, or handed to something that finishes later. The default is the opposite — the closure must be finished before the function returns — and that default is what lets Swift promise it cannot cause a leak.
whyWrong: Throwing is a separate matter, written with `throws`. The two have nothing to do with each other.
Giving back a value changes nothing. `map` takes a closure that returns something and it is still non-escaping.
Having parameters is irrelevant. What matters is only whether the closure survives the call.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums.map { $0 * 2 })
questions.explanation: `map` runs the closure on every item and builds a new list from the results, keeping the order. `$0` is just a short name for "the item we are on right now". So each number is doubled: `[2, 4, 6]`. The original list is untouched.
whyWrong: That is the list we started from. `map` does not change it — it makes a new one, which is what gets printed here.
12 would be the sum of the doubled values, which is what `reduce` does. `map` keeps one result per item.
`map` does not nest anything. Lists inside lists come from returning a list for each item, and here we return a number.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
var n = 1
let f = { [n] in print(n) }
n = 2
f()
questions.explanation: The `[n]` at the start is a capture list: it copies the value of `n` at the moment the closure is created, which is 1. From then on the closure has its own copy and no longer cares what happens to the original.
whyWrong: 2 is what you get **without** the capture list, because then the closure reads the variable fresh each time it runs.
`n` always holds a number: there is nothing optional in sight.
It builds. A capture list on a value type is ordinary, and it is exactly the way to freeze a value.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `@autoclosure` wraps `build()` in a closure instead of running it. Inside `log`, `enabled` is false, so `msg()` is never called — and `build` never runs. Nothing is printed at all, which is exactly the point of the feature.
whyWrong: `building` would be printed if `build()` ran. It does not: it was wrapped up and nobody asked for it.
Neither line is printed. `build` never runs, and `print(msg())` is inside an `if` that is false.
`x` is what `build` would hand back, but nothing is printed because the `if` is never entered.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Each call to `makeCounter` creates a brand new `c`, and the closure it returns keeps that one alive. So `a` and `b` have separate counters. `a` is called twice and reaches 2; `b` is called once and reaches 1.
whyWrong: 1 1 would mean each call started from scratch. The whole point is that the captured `c` survives between calls.
2 2 would mean `a` and `b` share one counter. They do not: each call to `makeCounter` made its own.
3 would mean `a` was called three times. It was called twice: once with `_ =`, once inside the `print`.

questions.prompt: Is a closure a value type or a reference type?
options: It depends on what it captures
questions.explanation: Closures are reference types. Assigning one to a new name does not copy it: both names are two ways to reach the same block, holding the same captured things. That is exactly why an escaping closure can create a retain cycle.
whyWrong: If it were a value type, assigning it would copy its captured variables too, and a shared counter like the one above could not work.
Copy-on-write belongs to `Array`, `String` and friends. Closures have nothing like it: there is nothing to copy on write.
It never depends: a closure is always a reference type, whether it captures anything or not.

questions.prompt: Do you need `[weak self]` in `items.map { self.format($0) }`?
options: No: the closure is non-escaping, so it cannot create a cycle
Yes, always, whenever you write self
Yes, otherwise it will not build
questions.explanation: `map` is non-escaping: its closure is guaranteed to be finished before `map` returns. A closure that cannot survive the call cannot keep anything alive, so there is no cycle to break. Writing `[weak self]` here would only add noise.
whyWrong: Not always. `[weak self]` is for escaping closures that something is also holding on to. Adding it everywhere makes the code harder to read, not safer.
It builds perfectly: in a non-escaping closure you can even leave out the word `self`.
Structs have nothing to do with it. Cycles only involve reference types, and the rule here is about escaping, not about kind.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The capture list copies **what is in the box**, and for a class that is the direction to the object, not the object. So the closure still reaches the same `C`, and sees `v` as 5. Capture lists freeze which object you are looking at, not what is inside it.
whyWrong: 0 would be true if the capture made a deep copy of the object. It does not: it copies the reference.
`v` is a normal `Int` starting at 0, so it can never be "nothing".
It builds. Putting a class instance in a capture list is allowed, and often it is exactly what you want.

questions.prompt: What happens if a closure with `[unowned self]` runs after the object has been freed?
options: `self` is nil and the block is skipped
questions.explanation: `unowned` is a promise you make to the compiler: "this object will still be there". It does not count as a holder and it is not optional, so there is no check. If the object is gone, reading it is reading freed memory and the app stops. `weak` is the safe version: it becomes `nil` and you handle it.
whyWrong: That is `weak`, which makes `self` optional precisely so you can check. `unowned` has no optional and no check.
Nothing stops the closure from running: it will run and then fail on the first use of `self`.
Nothing recreates a freed object. Once the memory is returned, it is gone.

topics.title: Collections: lists, sets and dictionaries
topics.summary: The three ways of holding many things at once, the handful of functions you use on them every day, and how to tell which one is slow.

lesson.heading: The three containers, and when each one fits
lesson.body:
When you have to keep several things together, Swift gives you three containers. They are not interchangeable: each is fast at something and slow at something else.

**`Array`** — things in a row, in the order you put them, duplicates allowed. Use it when the order matters, or when you will mostly walk through it from start to end. Written `[1, 2, 3]`.

**`Set`** — a bag of unique things, in no particular order. Putting something in twice does nothing. Use it when you need to ask "have I already seen this?", because that question is answered instantly however big the set is.

**`Dictionary`** — pairs of key and value, like a phone book: give it a name, get a number. Also instant, also unordered. Written `["a": 1]`.

Two small things you will use constantly. `insert` on a `Set` tells you whether the thing was actually new, so you can check and insert in one go. And on a `Dictionary`, `[key, default: 0]` means "if the key is missing pretend it was 0", which is what makes counting a one-liner instead of four.

lesson.heading: What it takes to go in a Set or be a key
lesson.body:
A `Set` and a `Dictionary` are fast because they do not search. They turn the value into a number — a **hash** — and use that number as an address: go straight there, look, done. No walking through everything.

That is why only types that are **`Hashable`** can go into a `Set` or be used as a key. `Hashable` means "I know how to turn myself into a number", and it builds on **`Equatable`**, "I know how to say whether I am the same as another one".

For your own structs you usually just write `: Hashable` and Swift writes both for you, from all the fields. You only do it by hand when "the same" means something narrower — for example two users are the same if their id matches, no matter what the rest says.

If you write it yourself, there is one rule you must not break: **two things that are equal must give the same hash**. If they do not, the set goes looking in the wrong place and loses things. The other direction is allowed: two different things may happen to give the same number, and the collection handles it.

lesson.heading: The functions you will use every day
lesson.body:
Instead of writing a loop and growing a result by hand, you say what you want. The code gets shorter and, more importantly, the name tells the reader what is going on.

**`map`** — one result for each item. The new list is always the same length.
**`filter`** — keep only the ones that pass a test. Shorter or equal.
**`reduce`** — boil everything down to a single value: a sum, a total, a dictionary.
**`compactMap`** — like `map`, but anything that comes out empty is dropped. This is the one for "convert these, keep the ones that worked".
**`flatMap`** — when each item gives you a small list, glue them into one flat list.
**`first(where:)`** — the first one that matches, and it stops looking straight away.
**`contains(where:)`**, **`allSatisfy`** — a yes-or-no answer about the whole collection.

One thing worth knowing about `reduce`: there are two versions. The plain one builds a fresh result at every step, which is fine for a number but wasteful when the result is a dictionary or an array — a copy per item. `reduce(into:)` keeps one result and changes it in place, so it does not copy.
lesson.code:
let ids = ["1", "x", "3"].compactMap { Int($0) }   // [1, 3] — "x" is dropped
let all = [[1, 2], [3]].flatMap { $0 }             // [1, 2, 3] — flattened
let sum = [1, 2, 3].reduce(0) { $0 + $1 }          // 6

// reduce(into:): one dictionary, changed in place
let freq = words.reduce(into: [:]) { result, word in
    result[word, default: 0] += 1
}

let firstLong = names.first { $0.count > 10 }      // stops at the first hit
let anyEmpty = names.contains { $0.isEmpty }       // true / false

lesson.heading: How fast is it, really
lesson.body:
The usual interview question is: how does the cost grow as the collection grows? There is a shorthand for it, and only a handful of cases to learn.

**Instant, whatever the size (O(1))** — reading `array[5]`, looking something up in a `Set` or `Dictionary`, appending to the end of an array. Appending is "almost always" instant: now and then the array runs out of room and moves everything into a bigger space, but because it asks for a lot of extra room at once, the average stays flat.

**Grows with the size (O(n))** — walking through everything, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `contains` on an **array**, and inserting or removing at the front, because every later item has to shuffle along.

The practical consequence worth remembering: if you are asking "is this in there?" inside a loop over an array, you are doing n times n work. Put the things in a `Set` first and the whole thing becomes n. That one swap is the most common fix for slow code at this level.

lesson.heading: Doing the work only when it is needed: lazy
lesson.body:
Chaining operations is readable, but each link builds a whole new list. `map` then `filter` over a million items means two million-item lists made and thrown away.

`.lazy` changes that. It builds no lists at all: it keeps the recipe, and only runs it on the items somebody actually asks for. Combine it with something that stops early — `first`, `first(where:)`, `prefix` — and you can leave almost all the work undone.

Beware of two things. First, `lazy` only pays off when you stop early or when the collection is big; on a short list, the extra bookkeeping costs more than it saves. Second, the closures run later, which makes anything with a side effect (a `print`, a counter) run in an order that can surprise you.

Two more everyday helpers worth knowing: `enumerated()`, which hands you the position along with the item, and `Dictionary(grouping:by:)`, which splits a list into buckets by a rule you give it — a contacts list by first letter, for example.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let r = ["1", "a", "3"].compactMap { Int($0) }
print(r)
questions.explanation: `Int("a")` cannot work, so it comes out empty. `compactMap` throws the empty ones away and opens the rest, so you get a clean `[Int]`: `[1, 3]`. With plain `map` you would have got `[Optional(1), nil, Optional(3)]`.
whyWrong: `nil` in the middle is what plain `map` would leave. Dropping it is the whole job of `compactMap`.
The `Optional(...)` wrappers are gone: `compactMap` opens the boxes as well as dropping the empty ones.
The results are numbers, not text. The closure converted them with `Int(...)`.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code: print([[1, 2], [3]].flatMap { $0 })
questions.explanation: The items here are themselves lists. `flatMap` takes each one and pours its contents into a single list, keeping the order. Two levels become one: `[1, 2, 3]`.
whyWrong: That is the list we started from, still nested. Flattening it is exactly what `flatMap` is for.
Nothing is repeated and nothing is counted: `flatMap` only joins, it does not change the values.
6 would be the sum, which is what `reduce` gives you. `flatMap` hands back a list, not a number.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `reduce` carries a running total, starting at 0. `$0` is that total and `$1` is the current item. At each step it adds double the item: 0+2, then +4, then +6, then +8, which comes to 20.
whyWrong: 10 is 1+2+3+4, the sum without doubling. Here each item is multiplied by 2 before being added.
18 does not come out of any reading of this. It is the kind of number you get by doubling only some of them.
12 would be the sum of only two doubled items. All four take part.

questions.prompt: How long does `contains` take on a `Set`, on average?
options: The same however big it is, O(1)
questions.explanation: A `Set` does not search. It turns the value into a number and goes straight to the matching spot. Ten items or ten million, the work is the same — and that is the whole reason to use a `Set` instead of an array.
whyWrong: Growing with the size is what happens on an **array**, which really does have to walk through its items.
O(log n) is what a sorted tree gives you, like a binary search. A `Set` does not sort anything.
O(n log n) is the cost of sorting. Looking something up has nothing to do with sorting.

questions.prompt: How much does `array.insert(x, at: 0)` cost?
options: It grows with the size, O(n)
questions.explanation: An array keeps its items in a row in memory. Making room at position 0 means moving every single item along by one. The longer the array, the longer it takes. Doing this in a loop is a classic way to make code slow without noticing.
whyWrong: It would be O(1) if there were a hole at the front. There is not: the first position is already taken.
O(log n) belongs to structures that cut the problem in half each time. An array does not.
"Almost always O(1)" is `append`, at the **end**. Pushing in at the front is a different story.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `default: 0` means "if the key is not there yet, treat it as 0", so the first `+= 1` works without any setup. In "banana" the letter a appears three times, so the answer is 3.
whyWrong: 1 would be the answer if each pass replaced the count instead of adding to it. `+=` adds.
2 is how many times n appears. Count the a's in b-a-n-a-n-a: positions 2, 4 and 6.
`nil` would mean the key is not in the dictionary. It is there, and `!` opens the box safely here.

questions.prompt: Which rule must a `Hashable` implementation never break?
options: Equal hashes mean the values are equal
Every value must have a unique hash
If two values are equal, their hashes must be equal
The hash must be the same every time the app runs
questions.explanation: The collection uses the hash to decide where to look. If two equal values produce different hashes, it looks in the wrong place and loses one of them. The other direction is fine: different values may share a hash, and the collection handles that by comparing properly.
whyWrong: That is the reverse, and it is not guaranteed: two different values can share a hash. The collection then falls back on `==`.
Unique hashes are impossible: there are far more possible values than there are numbers to hash them to. Collisions are normal.
It is deliberately **not** stable between runs: Swift mixes in a random seed each time, as protection against certain attacks. Never store a hash.

questions.prompt: What does `print(Set([3, 1, 2]))` print?
options: An error: a Set cannot be printed
The three numbers, in no guaranteed order
questions.explanation: A `Set` has no order at all: it stores things wherever their hash lands them. The order you see can even change between runs, because the hashing uses a fresh random seed each time. If you need an order, say so: `Set(...).sorted()`.
whyWrong: Sorted is what you get from `.sorted()`. A `Set` makes no such promise, even if it happens to come out that way once.
The order you put things in is not kept either: that is an `Array`'s job.
It prints fine. There is just no promise about the order.

questions.prompt: Which numbers does the `print` inside the closure show?
questions.explanation: `lazy` runs the work item by item, only as far as it has to. It tries 1 (gives 10, not above 15), then 2 (gives 20, which passes) and stops. 3 and 4 are never touched. Without `lazy` all four would be worked out first.
whyWrong: All four is what happens **without** `lazy`: the whole list is built before `first` even looks at it.
Something is printed: `first` does need values, so the chain runs — just only as far as necessary.
1 is reached too: it is tested first, and only fails the condition afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `reduce(into:)` over plain `reduce` when the result is a dictionary?
options: It is the only one that works with Dictionary
It changes one result in place instead of rebuilding it each step
It runs on several cores at once
It does not need a starting value
questions.explanation: Plain `reduce` hands you the running result and expects a new one back, so with a dictionary you end up copying it once per item. `reduce(into:)` gives you the same one each time and lets you change it directly, so there is nothing to copy.
whyWrong: Both work with any type. The difference is only in how the result is carried along.
Neither runs in parallel: both go through the items in order, one at a time.
Both need a starting value: `reduce(into: [:])` is giving one right there.

topics.title: Protocols and generics
topics.summary: How to describe what a type can do without caring which type it is, and how to write code that works with many types at once.

lesson.heading: A protocol is a list of promises
lesson.body:
A **protocol** does not do anything. It is a list: these are the properties and methods a type must have in order to call itself one of these.

Think of a job advert. "Must be able to speak English and drive". The advert does not speak or drive — it says what is required. Anyone who meets the requirements can apply, whoever they are.

A type that meets the list **conforms** to the protocol, and you write that with a colon. From then on you can write code against the protocol instead of against the type: it will work with anything that conforms, including things that did not exist when you wrote it.

The big difference from inheritance, which does something similar, is that **anything can conform**: structs, enums, classes. And it can conform to as many protocols as it likes, while a class can only inherit from one parent. This is why Swift leans on protocols where older languages lean on base classes.

lesson.heading: Giving a protocol a default implementation
lesson.body:
A protocol on its own cannot hold code. But you can **extend** it, and anything you write in that extension is available to every type that conforms, for free.

This is the heart of what people call protocol-oriented programming: the protocol says what is required, the extension provides the ready-made behaviour, and a conforming type only writes the bits that are genuinely its own.

There is a subtlety here that gets asked about constantly, and it has caught everybody out at least once.

If the method **is in the protocol's list**, and the type writes its own version, the type's version always wins, however you are holding the value.

If the method is **only in the extension** and not in the list, the protocol does not know it can be overridden. Then the version that runs depends on how you are holding the value: through the type you get the type's version, through the protocol you get the extension's.

The practical rule that avoids the whole mess: **if a type is meant to be able to replace it, put it in the protocol's list too**, not only in the extension.

lesson.heading: Generics: one piece of code, many types
lesson.body:
Writing the same function three times for `Int`, `String` and `Date` is tedious and it rots: fix a bug in one and you forget the other two.

**Generics** solve it. The letter in angle brackets, `<T>`, is a placeholder: "some type, and I do not care which, as long as it is the same one throughout". When you call the function, Swift works out what `T` actually is and builds a version for it. Nothing is decided while the app runs, so there is no cost at all.

Often you do need to care a little: to compare two things, they must be comparable. That is a **constraint**, written after the colon: `<T: Comparable>`. The protocol is used here as a requirement — "any type, as long as it can do this".

And you can constrain a whole extension, which is how you say things like "an array is printable, but only when its elements are".

lesson.heading: When the protocol itself needs a placeholder
lesson.body:
Sometimes the protocol cannot know what it is working with. A storage protocol can save things — but which things depends entirely on whoever conforms.

That is an **`associatedtype`**: a placeholder inside the protocol, filled in by the conforming type. `Collection` works exactly this way: it has an `Element`, and an array of numbers pins it to `Int`.

These protocols have a limitation that produces one of the most common error messages in Swift: you cannot write them as a plain type. `var s: Store` is refused, because "a store" is not enough — a store of what? Without knowing `Item`, the compiler cannot say whether `save(x)` is valid.

There are two ways round it. Use it as a constraint on a generic, which is what you want most of the time. Or pin the placeholder down in the type itself, written `some Collection<Int>` — "a collection, whose elements are numbers".

lesson.heading: some and any: two ways to hide a type
lesson.body:
Both words mean "I am not telling you the exact type". The difference is **who** does not know it.

**`some Shape`** — "there is one single real type here, it is decided when the code is compiled, and I am not telling you which". The caller does not know; the compiler does. That means no cost at all, and the type is the same on every call. If your function could return a circle or a square depending on a condition, `some` does not compile: that would be two different types.

**`any Shape`** — "it could be anything that conforms, and it can be different each time". The decision is made while the app runs, and the value travels in a box with a note on it saying what it really is. There is a small cost, and in exchange you can put circles and squares in the same array.

The rule of thumb: **`some` when there is only one type and you are hiding it; `any` when you genuinely need several different ones together.**

One last thing, because it is the most common error people hit. A protocol with `Self` in it — `Equatable` is the famous one — cannot be used with `any` in a comparison. `==` requires both sides to be the **same** type, and `any Equatable` only promises "something comparable", which may well be a date on one side and a number on the other. The answer is to use a generic, so both sides are pinned to one type.

questions.prompt: Where do you put a default implementation for a method listed in a protocol?
options: In a base class everything inherits from
In an extension of the protocol
questions.explanation: A protocol can only list requirements, not hold code. An extension of it can, and whatever you write there is given to every conforming type for free, unless that type writes its own version.
whyWrong: Inside the protocol you can only say what is required — the signature, without a body.
A base class would only work for classes, and would stop structs and enums conforming. An extension works for all three.
There is no such attribute in Swift. The mechanism is the extension.

questions.prompt: Which of these can NOT conform to `protocol Delegate: AnyObject`?
questions.explanation: `: AnyObject` on a protocol means "only classes may conform". A struct is a value type, so it is shut out. This is done on purpose for delegates: it lets the reference be held `weak`, which only works on classes, and that is what prevents the retain cycle.
whyWrong: `final` only means nobody may inherit from it. It is still a class, so it conforms happily.
`NSObject` and everything under it are classes, so they are allowed.
Being generic changes nothing: it is still a class.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `hi` is in the protocol's list, so the protocol knows a type may replace it. Which version runs is decided while the app runs, by looking at what the value really is. It is an `S`, so `S`'s version wins, even though you are holding it as a `Greeter`.
whyWrong: P would be the answer if `hi` existed only in the extension and not in the list. It is in the list.
It builds fine: `S` provides everything required.
Something is printed: `hi` is called and `S` has a body for it.

questions.prompt: What does a return type of `some View` tell you?
options: Any View, possibly a different one on each call
One single real type, picked when compiling and hidden from the caller
An optional that might be nil
questions.explanation: `some` means the type is decided once, while compiling, and always the same on every call — you are simply not told which. That is why it costs nothing and why a function returning `some View` cannot return a circle on one branch and a square on the other.
whyWrong: That is `any`: it allows a different type each time and is decided while the app runs.
There is no box. `some` is resolved when compiling, with no wrapper and no cost.
It has nothing to do with optionals. `some View` always holds a real view.

questions.prompt: What is an `associatedtype` in a protocol for?
options: To declare a generic parameter of a function
To leave a placeholder type that the conforming type fills in
questions.explanation: It is a blank the protocol leaves for the conforming type to fill in. `Collection` has `Element`: the protocol does not know what is inside, and an array of numbers decides it is `Int`.
whyWrong: A function's generic parameter is written in angle brackets on the function. `associatedtype` belongs to the protocol.
That is `: AnyObject`, which is a completely different thing.
`typealias` makes a nickname for a type that already exists. `associatedtype` leaves a blank to be filled later.

questions.prompt: How do you say that `Array` is `Printable`, but only when its elements are?
questions.explanation: `where` adds a condition to the extension: the conformance only exists when the elements themselves qualify. This is how a lot of the standard library is built — an array is `Equatable` only if its elements are.
whyWrong: That spelling would mean an array whose elements are literally the protocol, which is a different and much narrower thing.
`if` is not used in a type declaration. The word for conditions on an extension is `where`.
That extends the protocol, not the array, and it would add nothing to `Array` itself.

questions.prompt: What happens when you try to build this function?
options: It builds and gives back `any Shape`
It fails: the two returns are different real types
It builds, and the type is decided while the app runs
It builds only if `Shape` is a class
questions.explanation: `some Shape` promises **one single** real type, fixed when compiling. Here one branch gives a circle and the other a square, so there is no single answer and the build fails. Changing the return type to `any Shape` fixes it, at the cost of a small wrapper.
whyWrong: Swift does not quietly turn `some` into `any`: they mean different things, and you have to ask for the one you want.
With `some` nothing is decided while the app runs — that is the whole difference from `any`.
Whether `Shape` is a class or not changes nothing. The problem is that there are two different types.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: This time `hi` is **not** in the protocol's list — the protocol is empty. So the protocol has no idea a type might replace it, and the version chosen is decided purely by how you are holding the value. You are holding a `Greeter`, so the extension's version runs. This is the classic trap, and the fix is to put `hi` in the list.
whyWrong: S would win if `hi` were listed in the protocol. It is not, so `S.hi` is just a method of `S` that happens to share the name.
It builds: the protocol asks for nothing, so `S` conforms with no effort.
Something is printed: there is a `hi` to call, it is the extension's.

questions.prompt: Why does this function not build?
options: `==` needs both sides to be the same type, and `any` does not promise that
Boxed values cannot have static methods
questions.explanation: `Equatable` says "I can be compared with another of **my own** type". `any Equatable` only promises "something comparable", so one side could be a date and the other a number, and `==` between those does not exist. The fix is a generic: `func same<T: Equatable>(_ a: T, _ b: T)` forces both sides to be one type.
whyWrong: You are allowed to write `any Equatable` — it just does not give you enough to compare two of them.
`throws` has nothing to do with it: nothing here throws an error.
The problem is not static methods. It is that the two sides are not known to match.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `T` has to be one single type for both arguments. `2.5` can only be a `Double`, and the bare `3` is a literal that Swift is happy to read as a `Double` too. So `T` becomes `Double`, the answer is the `Double` 3, and printing it shows `3.0`.
whyWrong: A plain `3` would mean `T` became `Int`. It cannot: `2.5` would not fit.
2.5 is the smaller one, and the function asks for the larger.
It builds. It would not if you wrote `let x = 3` first, because then `3` would already be locked in as an `Int`.

topics.title: When something can go wrong
topics.summary: How a function says "this might fail", how you deal with it, and the small words — try?, try!, defer — that decide what happens next.

lesson.heading: throws: a function that might fail
lesson.body:
Some jobs can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your code: the network is down, the file is not there, the password is wrong. These are not bugs, they are normal outcomes you have to handle.

In Swift a function that can fail says so in its signature, with **`throws`**. That word is a promise to the reader and a rule for the compiler: nobody can call this function and pretend nothing could go wrong.

When you call one, you write **`try`** in front. The word does nothing at runtime — it is there so that anyone reading the code can see, at a glance, which lines might not finish.
