To actually handle the failure you wrap the call in **`do { } catch { }`**. If something is thrown, the rest of the `do` block is skipped and the matching `catch` runs instead.

What gets thrown is an ordinary value of any type that conforms to the `Error` protocol — usually an `enum`, because a failure normally has a handful of named shapes, and an enum can carry details inside each one. In the `catch` you can match on the exact case, and even add a `where` to split one case further. If no `catch` matches, the error carries on up to the caller.

lesson.heading: try? and try!: the two shortcuts
lesson.body:
Sometimes you do not care **why** it failed, only that it did. Writing a whole `do/catch` for that is noise, so there are two shorter forms.

**`try?`** turns a failure into nothing. The result becomes optional: a value if it worked, `nil` if it threw. The error itself is thrown away. Use it when the reason genuinely does not change what you do next — and remember that an error you silently discard is an error nobody will ever debug.

One detail that catches people out: if the function already returned an optional, `try?` does **not** give you a box inside a box. Swift flattens it, so `Int?` stays `Int?`.

**`try!`** says "this cannot fail, and if it does, stop the app". It is a deliberate crash. It is reasonable for something that can only fail if you made a mistake while writing — a regular expression you typed yourself, a file you shipped inside the app. It is never reasonable for anything that depends on the network, the disk, or the user.

The honest question to ask yourself before writing either: can I explain, in one sentence, why losing this information is fine?

lesson.heading: Result: a failure you can carry around
lesson.body:
`throws` works beautifully when the failure happens **now**, in the line you are reading. But sometimes the failure happens later and has to be carried: a completion handler, a value stored in a property, a list of outcomes.

That is what **`Result`** is for. It is an enum with two cases, `.success(value)` and `.failure(error)`, and because it is just a value you can keep it in a variable, put it in an array, or pass it to a closure.

You move between the two worlds easily. `try result.get()` turns a `Result` back into the throwing world: it hands you the value or throws the error inside. And `Result { try something() }` goes the other way, catching a throw into a value.

The practical rule nowadays: inside `async` code use `throws`, because it reads straight down the page. Reach for `Result` when the outcome has to be stored or passed around — and in older code based on completion handlers, which is still everywhere.

lesson.heading: rethrows, and saying which error
lesson.body:
**`rethrows`** is for functions that take a closure. `map` is the example: it does not fail on its own, but if the closure you hand it throws, that error has to come out.

Writing plain `throws` would force every caller to write `try`, even the ones whose closure cannot fail. `rethrows` says "I only throw if what you gave me throws", and the compiler then only demands `try` from the callers who need it.

The other newer thing is **typed throws**: `throws(LoadError)` instead of plain `throws`. It names exactly which error can come out, so in the `catch` you get that type instead of the vague `any Error` — which means you can switch over it and the compiler will tell you if you missed a case.

Use it where the set of failures is genuinely closed and small, such as a parser. For anything that touches the network or the file system, plain `throws` stays the honest choice, because you do not really know everything that can come back.

lesson.heading: defer: the tidying up that always happens
lesson.body:
When a function can leave through several doors — a normal `return`, an early `guard`, a thrown error — the tidying up has to happen on every one of them. Writing it before each exit means forgetting it somewhere.

**`defer`** fixes that. You write the clean-up once, next to the thing it cleans up, and Swift runs it when the current scope ends, whichever way it ends.

Two rules worth memorising:

**They run in reverse order.** The last `defer` written is the first to run, which is right: later work usually depends on earlier work, so it has to be undone first.

**They run before the `catch`.** If a function throws, its `defer` blocks run on the way out, and only then does the caller's `catch` get the error.

And one restriction: a `defer` block cannot leave the function. No `return`, no `throw`, no `break` out of it. It can print, it can call things, it can change local variables — but it cannot change where the function is going.

questions.prompt: Given `func f() throws -> Int`, what type is `try? f()`?
questions.explanation: `try?` turns a failure into nothing, so the result has to be able to hold "nothing": `Int?`. If `f` worked you get the number; if it threw you get `nil`, and the error itself is thrown away.
whyWrong: A plain `Int` would leave nowhere to put the failure. `try?` works precisely by making the result optional.
`Result` keeps the error. `try?` deliberately throws it away — that is the difference between the two.
There is no box in a box: `f` returns a plain `Int`, so one level of optional is enough.

questions.prompt: What happens if a function called with `try!` throws an error?
questions.explanation: `try!` is you promising the compiler that this cannot fail. If it does, the promise was wrong, and Swift stops the app on the spot rather than carrying on with nonsense. That is why it only belongs where failure would mean a mistake in your own code.
whyWrong: Getting `nil` is `try?`. The `!` version has no optional at all: it either succeeds or it stops everything.
Nothing is ignored. Quietly swallowing the error is what `try?` does.
It builds perfectly. The compiler takes your promise at face value — that is exactly the risk.

questions.prompt: What does `result.get()` do on a `Result<Int, MyError>`?
options: Returns the value, or throws the error it was holding
Waits until the result is ready
questions.explanation: `get()` is the bridge from the `Result` world back to the `throws` world. On a success it hands you the value; on a failure it throws the error inside. That is why you write `try result.get()`.
whyWrong: It does not hand back an optional: on failure it throws, which is more informative than `nil`.
It never hands you the error as a value. To look at the error without throwing, match on `.failure` instead.
There is no waiting involved: a `Result` already holds its outcome.

questions.prompt: Given `func g() throws -> Int?`, what type is `try? g()`?
questions.explanation: In older Swift this really did give `Int??`, and it was a nuisance. Since Swift 5 the levels are flattened: `try?` on something already optional stays at one level, `Int?`. You cannot tell apart "it threw" from "it returned nil", and in practice that is what you wanted anyway.
whyWrong: `Int??` was the old behaviour. It was deliberately flattened because nobody ever wanted the two levels.
A plain `Int` would leave nowhere to put either the failure or the `nil` that `g` can return.
`try?` hands back the value, not the error. The error is discarded.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `defer` blocks are kept aside and run when the scope ends, in reverse order of writing. So `print("3")` runs normally first, then the last `defer` written (2), then the first (1).
whyWrong: That would be the order if `defer` ran straight away. It does not: it waits for the end of the scope.
The order is reversed, not kept. The last one written is the first to run.
`print("3")` is not deferred at all, so it cannot come last.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Throwing ends `f`'s scope, so its `defer` runs on the way out: `cleanup` is printed first. Only then does the error reach the caller, and `caught` is printed. This ordering is what makes `defer` safe for closing files and connections.
whyWrong: The order is the other way round: the `defer` belongs to `f`, which finishes before the caller ever sees the error.
`cleanup` is not skipped. A `defer` runs on every way out, throwing included — that is the whole point.
`caught` is printed too: the error does leave `f` and the `catch` does receive it.

questions.prompt: What does `rethrows` mean in a signature?
options: It always rethrows whatever it receives
It turns errors into a Result
It throws only if the closure you passed in throws
It tries the operation again on failure
questions.explanation: It is for functions that take a closure and have no failures of their own. It passes the promise on: if your closure cannot fail, the caller does not need to write `try`. `map` and `filter` work exactly this way.
whyWrong: "Always" is wrong: if nothing is handed in that can throw, the function cannot throw either, and the compiler knows it.
There is no conversion to `Result`. That would be a different thing you write yourself.
Nothing is retried. `rethrows` says who can fail, not what to do about it.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The `catch` blocks are tried from the top down. The first matches the case but its `where` demands 500 or more, and 404 is not, so it is skipped. The second matches with no extra condition, so it runs.
whyWrong: `server` would need `c >= 500`. 404 does not pass that test, so that block is skipped.
The bare `catch` at the end is only reached if nothing above matched. The second one did.
It builds: matching an error's case, with or without a `where`, is ordinary Swift.

questions.prompt: With `func load() throws(LoadError)`, what type is `error` inside the `catch`?
questions.explanation: That is the whole point of typed throws: you name which error can come out, so the `catch` gets that exact type instead of the vague `any Error`. You can then switch over its cases and the compiler will tell you if you missed one.
whyWrong: `any Error` is what you get from a plain `throws`, where anything at all might come out.
There is no optional involved: inside a `catch` there is always an error.
`NSError` is an Objective-C type. Swift errors are whatever type you declared.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT allowed inside a `defer` block?
questions.explanation: A `defer` runs while the function is already on its way out. If it could `return` or `throw`, it would change where the function is going after that was already decided, and the order of several `defer` blocks would become impossible to reason about. So Swift forbids it.
whyWrong: Calling functions is the usual content of a `defer`: closing a file, unlocking a lock.
Changing a local variable is allowed, and is sometimes exactly what you want.
Printing is allowed, and is the easiest way to see the reverse order for yourself.

topics.title: Memory: who keeps an object alive
topics.summary: How Swift decides when to free an object, why two objects can keep each other alive forever, and the three words that fix it.

lesson.heading: Counting who is holding on
lesson.body:
When you create a class instance, Swift reserves memory for it. That memory has to be given back when nobody needs it any more — otherwise the app grows until the system kills it.

Swift decides this by **counting**. Every object carries a number: how many places are currently holding a reference to it. Store it in a variable, the number goes up. That variable goes away or is set to `nil`, the number goes down. When it reaches zero, the object is freed immediately and its `deinit` runs.

This is called **ARC**, automatic reference counting. "Automatic" means the compiler writes the up and down for you — you never type them.

Two things are worth being clear about:

**It is immediate, not a sweep.** Unlike the garbage collectors in Java or C#, there is no pause and no separate thread. The moment the count hits zero, the memory is gone. That makes the timing predictable, which matters a lot on a phone.

**It only applies to references.** Structs, enums and numbers are copied, so nobody needs to count them. ARC concerns class instances and the memory a closure uses to hold what it captured.

lesson.heading: strong, weak, unowned
lesson.body:
Every reference is **strong** unless you say otherwise. Strong means it counts: as long as it exists, the object cannot be freed.

**`weak`** does not count. It is a way of saying "I want to reach this, but I am not the reason it is alive". When the object is freed, ARC quietly sets every weak reference to it to `nil` — which is why a `weak` property must be `var` and must be optional. There is nowhere else for the `nil` to go.

**`unowned`** also does not count, but it has no optional and no check. It is you telling the compiler "this will still be there when I look". If you are wrong, the app stops. Use it only when the two lifetimes are tied together by construction — a credit card that cannot exist without its owner.

The practical order to think in: strong by default, `weak` when the thing might go away first, `unowned` only when you can explain in one sentence why it cannot.

lesson.heading: Two objects that keep each other alive
lesson.body:
Here is the problem counting cannot solve on its own. A holds B strongly, and B holds A strongly. Even when nothing else in the app refers to either of them, each one's count is still 1 — because of the other. Neither is ever freed. That is a **retain cycle**, and it is a leak.

The classic place this appears is the delegate pattern. A list view holds its delegate so it can tell it things; the delegate is usually the screen that owns the list. Each holds the other, and the whole screen leaks every time you open it.

The fix is a rule you can apply without thinking: **a child never holds its parent strongly**. The list holds its delegate `weak`.

For this to be possible the protocol has to be class-only, written `: AnyObject`. Without that, Swift refuses the `weak`, because a struct has no reference to make weak — and the error message is one of the most common in the language.

lesson.heading: Cycles made by closures
lesson.body:
The other half of all leaks comes from closures. A closure that escapes holds everything it captured, strongly. So if an object stores a closure, and that closure mentions the object, you have the same loop as before.

The fix is the capture list: `[weak self]`. Inside the closure `self` becomes optional, so you usually open it straight away with `guard let self else { return }`. If the object has gone, there is nothing to do and you leave.

The part worth getting right is **when you actually need it**, because sprinkling `[weak self]` everywhere makes code harder to read for no benefit:

**Not needed** when the closure is non-escaping — `map`, `sorted`, `forEach`. It cannot survive the call, so it cannot keep anything alive.

**Not needed** for a one-shot closure handed to something that lets go afterwards, such as `DispatchQueue.main.async`. It holds `self` for a moment, runs, and releases. That delays the free, it does not prevent it.

**Needed** when the object itself stores the closure, or hands it to something it also holds: a property, a subscription, an observer.

lesson.heading: Finding a leak, and the ones that hide
lesson.body:
The quickest check costs nothing: put a `print` in `deinit`. Open the screen, close it, and if nothing is printed, something is still holding on.

For the real answer there is the **Memory Graph Debugger** in Xcode: pause the app, press the button with the three linked nodes, and you get a picture of every live object and who is pointing at it. Cycles show up as a loop you can see with your eyes. Instruments' Leaks tool does the same from a different angle.

Two leaks that `[weak self]` does **not** fix, because the cycle is not where you think:

**A repeating `Timer`.** The run loop holds the timer, and the timer holds its block. Even with `[weak self]`, the timer itself never dies. You have to call `invalidate()`, usually when the screen goes away.

**Observers and subscriptions.** `NotificationCenter` with a block, a Combine `AnyCancellable`, a KVO token: each has to be stored and released. Storing them in a property of the screen is usually enough, because then they die with it.

questions.prompt: What does ARC actually count?
options: Class instances and what closures capture
questions.explanation: Counting only makes sense for things that can be shared, and only references are shared. Structs, enums and numbers are copied, so each owner has their own and there is nothing to count.
whyWrong: Structs are not counted: they are copied. A struct only takes part indirectly, when it holds a class inside it.
ARC is Swift's own mechanism and works on pure Swift classes, with no Objective-C anywhere in sight.
Where a variable lives changes nothing. What matters is whether the value is a reference.

questions.prompt: Why does a `weak` property have to be optional?
options: Because weak only works with protocols
Because ARC writes nil into it when the object is freed
So that it can be set later
It is a convention, not a rule
questions.explanation: A weak reference does not keep the object alive, so the object can disappear while you are still pointing at it. ARC then has to put something there, and the only honest answer is `nil`. That is also why it has to be `var`: ARC needs to be able to write to it.
whyWrong: `weak` works with any class reference, protocol or not. What it does need is that the thing is a class.
Setting it later is what any optional allows. The reason here is specifically that ARC clears it.
It is a hard rule: a non-optional `weak` does not compile.

questions.prompt: Which Xcode tool shows you the live objects and who is pointing at them?
questions.explanation: Pause the app and press the memory graph button: you get every live object and every arrow between them. A retain cycle appears as a visible loop, which is the fastest way to find one.
whyWrong: The View Debugger shows the layers of the interface, not who owns what in memory.
The Time Profiler shows where the time goes, which is a different question.
That one simulates a slow network. Nothing to do with memory.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: `w` is weak, so it does not count. The only strong holder is `a`, and setting it to `nil` drops the count to zero: the object is freed at once and `bye` is printed. ARC then clears `w`, so the comparison prints `true`.
whyWrong: `false` would mean `w` is still pointing at something. ARC clears every weak reference the moment the object goes.
The order is wrong: freeing comes first, and the print on the last line comes after.
`false` is wrong for the reason above, even though the order here is right.

questions.prompt: Why does `weak var delegate: MyDelegate?` not build?
options: The protocol is not limited to classes
questions.explanation: `weak` works on a reference, and only classes have one. If the protocol can also be adopted by a struct, there is nothing to make weak. Writing `protocol MyDelegate: AnyObject` restricts it to classes and the error goes away.
whyWrong: It is the opposite: `weak` must be `var`, because ARC has to be able to write `nil` into it.
`weak` requires an optional, it does not forbid one.
`@objc` belongs to the Objective-C world and is not needed for this at all.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this class?
options: Nothing: closures capture weakly by default
A cycle: VM holds the closure and the closure holds VM
questions.explanation: `onUpdate` is a property, so the object holds the closure strongly. The closure mentions `self`, so it holds the object strongly. Each keeps the other alive and the count never reaches zero. `[weak self]` in the closure breaks it.
whyWrong: Closures capture strongly by default, which is exactly how this cycle happens.
A closure stored in a property is `@escaping` automatically: on a property type you do not write it.
`refresh` is only called when somebody calls `onUpdate`. The problem is memory, not repetition.

questions.prompt: Does `DispatchQueue.main.async { self.update() }` create a permanent cycle?
options: No: the queue lets the block go once it has run
Yes, for as long as the app is open
No, because the main queue uses weak references
questions.explanation: The queue holds the block, the block holds `self`, but only until it has run — then the queue releases it and the count drops. The object's death is delayed by a moment, which is not a leak. `self` is not holding the queue, so there is no loop.
whyWrong: Not always. `[weak self]` matters when something the object owns holds the closure; here the queue owns it and lets go.
The block is released as soon as it has run, not when the app closes.
The queue does hold the block strongly. What saves you is that it releases it afterwards.

questions.prompt: When is `unowned` the right choice instead of `weak`?
options: When the object may vanish at any moment
When the object referred to lives at least as long as the one referring
questions.explanation: `unowned` has no check and no optional: if the object is gone, reading it stops the app. So it is only safe when the lifetimes are tied by construction — a credit card that cannot exist without its owner. In exchange you avoid the optional dance.
whyWrong: That is exactly when you must use `weak`: `unowned` would crash.
A delegate is the typical case for `weak`, because the delegate can perfectly well go away first.
Neither word applies to structs: there is no reference to count.

questions.prompt: If the object is already freed, what is the difference between `unowned` and `unowned(unsafe)`?
options: `unowned` stops the app on purpose; `unsafe` reads rubbish
None, they are the same thing
questions.explanation: `unowned` keeps enough bookkeeping to notice the object has gone, and stops the app deliberately — a clear crash you can debug. `unowned(unsafe)` keeps nothing: it reads the old address whatever is there now, which may be garbage or another object entirely. That is the worst kind of bug.
whyWrong: Neither becomes `nil`. Only `weak` does that.
`unowned` is not optional, so it cannot be `nil`. It stops the app instead.
They are genuinely different: one is a controlled stop, the other is undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: With `[weak self]` the controller is freed, but the timer keeps ticking. What is missing?
options: Call invalidate: the run loop is holding the timer
questions.explanation: `[weak self]` solves the controller's leak, but not the timer's life. A repeating timer is held by the run loop, not by you, so it keeps firing with `self` already `nil`. You have to call `invalidate()`, usually when the screen goes away.
whyWrong: It does not cover it: the controller is freed, but the timer is still alive and still firing.
`unowned` would make it worse: once the controller is gone, the next tick would stop the app.
`@objc` is only needed for the old selector-based timer, and it has nothing to do with this.

topics.title: Doing more than one thing at a time
topics.summary: async/await, tasks, actors and @MainActor: how to wait for something slow without freezing the app, and how to avoid two pieces of code fighting over the same data.

lesson.heading: Why async/await exists
lesson.body:
Some jobs are slow: downloading, reading a big file, talking to a database. If you do them on the **main thread** — the one that draws the interface and reacts to taps — everything freezes. The user sees a dead screen.

So the slow work has to happen somewhere else, and you have to be told when it is done. For years the answer was the completion handler: hand over a closure and get called back. It works, but with three or four steps you end up with blocks inside blocks, every error handled by hand, and an easy way to forget one path entirely.

**async/await** says the same thing in a straight line. A function marked `async` is one that may pause. At the point where it waits, you write `await`, and the code below simply carries on after.

The key thing to understand, and it is the question that gets asked: **`await` does not block the thread**. The function is suspended and put aside; the thread goes off and does other work; when the result arrives the function is picked up again, possibly on a different thread. Nothing is standing still waiting.

lesson.heading: Tasks, and running things side by side
lesson.body:
`async` code has to start somewhere. `Task { }` is the door from normal code into the async world: it starts a piece of work and lets the current function carry on.

Two `await` one after the other happen **in sequence**: the second only starts when the first has finished. If the two jobs do not depend on each other, that is wasted time.

To run them side by side you write **`async let`**. The work starts immediately, and the `await` comes later, where you actually need the result. Two downloads of one second each take one second in total instead of two.

This is called **structured concurrency**, and the structure gives you three things for free. The parent does not finish until its children have. Cancelling the parent cancels the children. And an error from a child comes up to the parent. You get no dangling work nobody is watching.

`Task.detached` steps outside all of that: no parent, no inherited priority, no inherited actor. You need it very rarely, and most uses of it are a mistake.

lesson.heading: Actors: one at a time, by construction
lesson.body:
The hardest bug in concurrent code is the **data race**: two pieces of code touching the same variable at the same time, one writing while the other reads. The result is nonsense, and it only happens on some runs, on some devices, which makes it nearly impossible to reproduce.

The old answer was a lock you remembered to take. The Swift answer is the **actor**: a type that guarantees only one piece of code is inside it at any moment. You cannot forget, because the compiler enforces it.

The price is that you have to `await` to get in, from outside. That `await` is Swift saying "somebody else might be inside right now; you may have to wait your turn".

And here is the trap that gets asked about in every senior interview. An actor protects you **between** awaits, not across them. If a method inside an actor awaits something, it gives up its turn: other calls can come in and change the state. When your method wakes up, anything it checked before the `await` may no longer be true. The rule: **check again after awaiting, or do not await between the check and the change**.

lesson.heading: @MainActor: the interface, always on its own thread
lesson.body:
The interface may only be touched from the main thread. Doing it from anywhere else gives you glitches, missing redraws and crashes that happen once a week.

**`@MainActor`** is the actor that *is* the main thread. Mark something with it and Swift guarantees it only runs there — and tells you off at compile time if you try otherwise. That turns a whole category of runtime bug into a message on your screen while you type.

You can mark a single method, a whole class, or a property. Marking the view model class is the usual choice: every property and method is then on the main thread, so updating what the screen shows is always safe.

There is no cost in the common case. If you are already on the main thread, calling a `@MainActor` method is a direct call with no hop. The hop only happens when you are genuinely somewhere else.

The pattern that follows from this: do the slow work off the main actor, then come back to it only to publish the result.

lesson.heading: Sendable and cancellation
lesson.body:
If a value can travel from one task to another, it must be safe to share. **`Sendable`** is the protocol that says so, and the compiler checks it for you.

What counts as safe: anything that cannot change, or that is copied rather than shared. A struct of `let` numbers and text is `Sendable` automatically. A `final class` whose every property is `let` can be, because nobody can change it. A class with a `var` cannot, unless it protects itself — which is exactly what an actor is.

The other thing to know is **cancellation**, because the behaviour surprises people. `task.cancel()` does not stop anything. It raises a flag. Your code has to look at that flag and decide to stop: `try Task.checkCancellation()` throws if it has been set, and `Task.isCancelled` just asks. Apple's own async functions already check it, which is why cancelling a download usually does work. In a long loop of your own, nothing happens unless you look.

questions.prompt: Does an `await` block the thread the function is running on?
options: Yes, but only on the main thread
No: the function is suspended and the thread is freed
questions.explanation: This is the whole point. At an `await` the function is put aside and the thread goes off to do other work. When the result is ready the function is resumed, possibly on a different thread. Nothing is standing still, which is why the interface keeps responding.
whyWrong: `DispatchQueue.sync` really does block: the thread stands there waiting. `await` was built to avoid exactly that.
The main thread behaves the same as any other here: it is freed, which is what keeps the app responsive.
Priority decides what runs first, not whether a thread is blocked.

questions.prompt: What happens when you try to build this?
options: It builds and increments straight away
It fails: calling `inc()` from outside needs `await`
It builds only in Swift 5 mode
questions.explanation: An actor lets one piece of code in at a time, so coming from outside you may have to wait your turn — and waiting is spelled `await`. The compiler enforces it, which is how it stops races before the app ever runs.
whyWrong: Nothing about an actor is immediate from outside: the whole point is that you might have to queue.
The race is exactly what the compiler is preventing here by refusing to build.
Swift 5 mode may soften some concurrency warnings, but calling an actor's method without `await` is an error either way.

questions.prompt: What does marking a class `@MainActor` mean?
options: It can only be created once
It can only be used from SwiftUI
Its properties and methods only run on the main thread
questions.explanation: `@MainActor` is the actor that *is* the main thread. Marking a class puts everything in it there, and the compiler tells you at build time if you try to touch it from somewhere else — which is why it is the natural home for a view model.
whyWrong: Nothing stops you making as many as you like. That would be a singleton, a different idea.
The methods stay exactly as you wrote them. What changes is only where they run.
It works in UIKit too, and in any Swift code at all.

questions.prompt: How do `fetchA()` and `fetchB()` run here?
options: One after the other, A then B
Only at the `await`, one after the other
Side by side, as children of this task
questions.explanation: `async let` starts the work straight away, so both are already running by the time you reach the `await`. They are children of the current task, which means cancelling the parent cancels them and an error from either comes up here.
whyWrong: One after the other is what plain `await` on each line would give you. `async let` exists precisely to avoid that.
Detached means no parent and no inherited context, and that is `Task.detached`, not `async let`.
Nothing waits for the `await` to start: the work began at the `async let`.

questions.prompt: What does `Task.detached` NOT inherit, compared with `Task { }`?
options: The actor, the priority and task-local values
questions.explanation: `Task { }` inherits the context it was started in: the actor it is on, the priority, task-local values. `Task.detached` inherits none of that and has no parent. The commonest consequence is that code which used to be on the main actor quietly is not any more.
whyWrong: Both can throw: that depends on what you write inside them.
Globals have nothing to do with it: both can reach them, which is itself a reason to be careful.
Both can be cancelled. The difference is that a detached task is not cancelled by its parent, because it has none.

questions.prompt: What does `task.cancel()` actually do?
options: Raises a flag that the task has to look at
Throws an error where it was called
Removes the task from the queue without running it
questions.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: nothing is interrupted by force, because stopping code halfway could leave things in a broken state. `cancel()` sets a flag, and your code notices it with `Task.isCancelled` or `try Task.checkCancellation()`. Apple's own async functions already check.
whyWrong: Nothing is stopped by force. A task killed mid-write could leave half-written data behind.
The error, if any, appears inside the task when it checks, not at the call to `cancel()`.
If the task has already started it carries on until it notices the flag.

questions.prompt: Which of these is `Sendable` without you doing anything?
options: `struct P { let x: Int; let name: String }`
questions.explanation: A struct whose parts are all constant and all themselves safe is `Sendable` automatically: it is copied, so two tasks never touch the same one. Numbers and text qualify, so the whole thing does.
whyWrong: A `var` in a class means two tasks could write to the same place at once. Not safe.
Without `final` somebody could subclass it and add a `var`, so Swift cannot promise anything.
`NSMutableArray` can be changed from anywhere, so the struct holding it is not safe either.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run `DispatchQueue.main.sync { }` while already on the main thread?
options: It is put off until the next loop
questions.explanation: `sync` means "stop here until the block has run on that queue". But the queue you are waiting for is the one you are standing on, and it cannot start the block until you let go. Each waits for the other, and the app is stuck for good.
whyWrong: It would run immediately only if the queue were free. It is not: you are occupying it.
`sync` never defers anything: deferring is `async`, which here would be perfectly safe.
There is no warning. It builds without complaint and freezes when it runs.

questions.prompt: Why can this method push the balance below zero?
options: Other calls can get in during the `await`
`guard` does not work inside an actor
questions.explanation: An actor guarantees one at a time **between** awaits, not across them. At the `await` this method gives up its turn, and another `withdraw` can come in, pass the same check and take the money. When the first one wakes up, its check is out of date. The fix is to check again after awaiting, or not to await between the check and the change.
whyWrong: They protect them very well — but only while you are actually holding the turn.
`guard` works exactly as everywhere else. The problem is when it was evaluated.
Nothing is copied: there is one `balance`, inside the actor.

questions.prompt: In what order do results arrive from `for await r in group`?
options: In the order the tasks were added
In a random but repeatable order
questions.explanation: A task group hands you each result the moment it is ready, so the fastest child comes first whatever order you added them in. If you need them back in the original order, send an index along with each result and sort afterwards.
whyWrong: That would mean waiting for the first one before showing the second, which throws away the point of running them together.
There is nothing random about it: it depends on how long each child actually takes.
They arrive one by one, which is what lets you show the first result straight away.
